planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; PowWow Wildberry is a compact, seed-grown coneflower that flowers reliably in its first year from an early sowing, unlike many coneflowers that need a full season to establish before blooming.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. PowWow Wildberry won an All-America Selections award for its ability to flower heavily from seed in its very first year, along with a notably compact habit that keeps the plant shorter and sturdier than older tall coneflower selections. The flowers are a deep rosy-purple with a slightly upturned, more horizontal petal form than the wild species, held over a long bloom season from early summer well into fall. Like other coneflowers it is drought-tolerant and attractive to butterflies and bees once established, and leaving the spent seed heads standing through winter provides food for goldfinches.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Caradonna is prized for its nearly black flower stems, which contrast dramatically with the violet-blue flowers and remain ornamental even after the petals fade.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Caradonna is one of the most widely planted hardy salvias, valued for its slender, nearly black flower stems topped with dense spikes of rich violet-blue flowers that create a striking two-tone vertical accent through the front and middle of a sunny border. Shearing the plant back by about half after the first flush of bloom encourages a strong second and sometimes third round of flowers into late summer. It is drought-tolerant once established, rarely bothered by deer or rabbits, and draws bees and hummingbirds throughout its long bloom season; in hot, humid zone 9 summers it may decline and is best treated as a shorter-lived perennial refreshed every few years.

common_name: East Friesland Salvia (Classic Compact Purple Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; East Friesland is an older, well-proven German-bred cultivar known for reliable rebloom when sheared after the first flush of flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Introduced from German breeding decades ago, East Friesland was one of the first widely available compact hardy salvias and remains a dependable garden standard, producing dense, upright spikes of rich reddish-purple flowers over a tidy, low mound of aromatic gray-green foliage. Shearing the spent flower spikes back by about half in early summer prompts a strong second flush of bloom later in the season. It is drought-tolerant, deer- and rabbit-resistant, and a strong bee and butterfly attractant, making it a reliable front-of-border choice, though it may act as a shorter-lived perennial in the hot, humid summers of zone 9.

common_name: Dutch Chocolate Baptisia (Decadence Series Bronze-Flowered False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Dutch Chocolate is part of the compact Decadence breeding series, bred to fit smaller garden spaces than the tall, sprawling wild Baptisia species while keeping the plant's legendary toughness and longevity.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Dutch Chocolate is a compact hybrid selection from the Decadence breeding series, developed to bring Baptisia's celebrated toughness, long lifespan, and pollinator appeal into a smaller, tidier plant better suited to modern garden borders than the tall, wide-spreading straight species. In late spring it produces dense spikes of unusual smoky maroon-brown flowers with a subtle chocolate cast, followed by ornamental dark seed pods that persist into fall. Like all baptisias it develops a deep taproot and resents being moved once established, so choose its planting site carefully; established plants are extremely drought-tolerant, essentially pest-free, and improve for many years without needing division.

common_name: Overdam Feather Reed Grass (Variegated Upright Reed Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Overdam is a variegated sport of Karl Foerster feather reed grass, staying slightly shorter and less vigorous than its parent, with cream-edged leaf blades that provide season-long color contrast.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Overdam arose as a variegated sport of the popular Karl Foerster feather reed grass, sharing the same stiffly upright, non-invasive clumping habit but with narrow leaf blades edged in creamy white that brighten through the season, sometimes taking on a pink flush in cool fall weather. Feathery, upright flower plumes appear in early summer, aging to a warm buff tan that stands well through winter for structural interest. It tolerates heavier clay soils and somewhat more shade than most ornamental grasses, and like its parent is sterile, posing no invasive seeding risk. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.
